topic: Texas option period: why 10 days is really 6
hook: Buyers pay for 10 option days. Most only get 6.

scores.worst_problem: The hook states the arithmetic conclusion outright (10 becomes 6), so a savvy buyer can half-guess the payoff — scheduling and report lag — before swiping.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 1 to withhold the number, e.g. "You paid for 10 option days. Your inspector already took most of them." — keep the loss vivid but the size and cause unstated.

deck.topic: Texas option period: why 10 days is really 6
deck.hook: Buyers pay for 10 option days. Most only get 6.

points.title: The Clock Never Pauses
body: Your option period runs on calendar days.
Saturdays, Sundays and holidays all count against you.

points.title: Six Days, Not Ten
body: The inspectors worth hiring are booked two to three days out.
Add another day for the written report to actually land in your inbox.
Ten paid days just became six real ones.
points.loop: Those six are not yours either.

points.title: Bids Eat The Rest
body: A foundation note means you now need a structural engineer.
Roofers and plumbers quote on their schedule, not on yours.

points.title: The Seller Sees Your Deadline
body: Your expiration date is written in the contract they are holding.
Ask for repairs on day nine and they can simply wait you out.

points.title: You Can Buy Time
body: Extensions are allowed, and they cost you real money.
They also have to be signed before the clock hits zero.
One hour late and that fee buys you nothing.

linkedinCaption:
A 10-day option period in Texas is not 10 working days. It runs on calendar days, so weekends and holidays count.

Good inspectors are usually booked two to three days out. Add a day for the written report. You are down to about six usable days before you have made a single decision.

Then the specialists arrive. A foundation note means a structural engineer. Roofers and plumbers quote on their own schedule.

The seller holds the same contract and knows your expiration date. Bring repair requests on day nine and waiting you out is a reasonable strategy for them.

Extensions exist. They cost money and must be signed before the clock hits zero.

For agents here: how early are you scheduling inspections relative to execution?
